A paraphrase is a restatement of something someone said or wrote, using different words, while keeping the exact same meaning.

Think of it like this: the clothing changes, but the body underneath stays identical.

Original sentence:
"The elderly man walked slowly across the road."

A paraphrase of it:
"The old man crossed the street at a slow pace."

Notice what happened — the words are different, the sentence is structured differently, but the meaning is perfectly preserved. That is a paraphrase.

For something to qualify as a paraphrase, it must do two things at once:

  1. Change the wording — you use your own words, not the original speaker's or writer's words.
  2. Preserve the meaning — the idea, information, or message must remain unchanged. Not even a small part of it.

If you fail condition 1, you have a quotation (exact original words).
If you fail condition 2, you have a distortion (a changed or misrepresented meaning) — and that is no longer a paraphrase.
How a Paraphrase Differs from Similar Things

This is where most learners get confused, so pay close attention.

Paraphrase vs. Quotation
A quotation reproduces the exact original words, usually placed inside quotation marks. A paraphrase rewrites those words freshly. So: "She said, 'I am exhausted'" is a quotation. "She mentioned that she was very tired" is a paraphrase.

Paraphrase vs. Summary
A summary is shorter than the original. It compresses and leaves things out, keeping only the main points. A paraphrase, however, is roughly the same length as the original — it doesn't cut anything out. It just re-expresses everything in new words. You can think of it this way: a summary is a shortcut, while a paraphrase is a detour that covers all the same ground.

Paraphrase vs. Translation
A translation converts text from one language to another. A paraphrase stays within the same language but changes the words used. However, here is an interesting nuance: people sometimes loosely call a translation a paraphrase too, especially when the translation is loose and expressive rather than word-for-word. But strictly speaking, the two are different things.

A paraphrase is used in many real-life situations:

  • To simplify — when the original is too complex or technical, a paraphrase makes it easier to understand. A doctor might paraphrase a medical report for a patient in plain language.
  • To clarify — in a conversation, you might paraphrase what someone said to make sure you understood them correctly: "So what you're saying is…"
  • To avoid plagiarism — in academic writing, instead of copying someone's words directly, a student paraphrases them to show their own understanding, while still crediting the source.
  • To adapt tone — the original might be too formal or too casual for a particular audience. A paraphrase can adjust the register while keeping the meaning.
A Closer Look at What Changes and What Doesn't

When you create a paraphrase, you are free to change:

  • The specific words (using synonyms or entirely different phrasing)
  • The sentence structure
  • The order in which ideas are expressed (within reason)
  • The voice (active vs. passive)

But you must not change:

  • The core meaning
  • The factual content
  • The intent behind what was said

Here is a longer original passage and then a paraphrase, so you can see the concept at work on a bigger scale.

Original:
"The scientists concluded that regular physical activity significantly reduces the risk of developing heart disease, and they strongly recommended that adults engage in at least thirty minutes of moderate exercise on most days of the week."

Paraphrase:
"Researchers found that exercising regularly can greatly lower a person's chances of getting heart disease, and they advised that most adults should do moderate physical activity for at least half an hour on the majority of days."

Every detail is preserved. No information is lost. No new information is added. Only the words and sentence structure are different.

A paraphrase is not just swapping a few words with synonyms while keeping the rest of the sentence the same. That is called patchwriting, and it is considered poor practice (and often a form of plagiarism in academic settings). A true paraphrase involves genuinely reconstructing the idea from scratch in your own words and your own sentence structure.

A paraphrase is your own fresh re-expression of someone else's idea, using different words, while being completely faithful to their original meaning — no more, no less. It is longer than a summary, freer than a quotation, and always stays within the same language. Its purpose is to restate, clarify, simplify, or adapt — without ever distorting.
